publication.subtitle: Open Access Modelling of the ASEAN Power Grid with TZ-APG
author: Vu, T.
Shivakumar, A.
Suarez, I.
Puspitarini, H. D.
Majid, A.

description: Business-as-usual continuation of existing ASEAN power and transmission systems.
pathwayDescription:
The Business-as-Usual (BAU) scenario in TransitionZero’s TZ-APG v1 model depicts the ASEAN region’s power system as it operates under prevailing infrastructure and national policy conditions through 2035. Built on the PyPSA modeling framework, this scenario assumes all existing domestic and cross-border transmission lines remain in place with their present capacities, and no new interconnectors are added. The pathway thus mirrors the current structural reality of the ASEAN Power Grid.

Under the static grid environment in BAU, each country continues to meet rising demand primarily through national generation expansion rather than regional power exchange. Power flows remain unidirectional and modest, constrained by limited physical connectivity and the lack of integrated market frameworks. The scenario also maintains a conservative technology palette (coal, gas, hydropower, solar, and wind) consistent with current ASEAN deployment trends.

A distinctive feature of TZ-APG v1 is that capacity and generation outcomes by 2035 vary only marginally across all four grid pathways. This underscores that the central focus of this study is not on changing generation composition but on understanding how different grid architectures affect system operation, investment distribution, and interregional dynamics. In BAU, this manifests as limited regional trade potential and continued reliance on domestic fossil resources.

coreDrivers.policies: Target technology shares: minimum RE/solar shares for Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines are imposed as constraints. Target capacity levels: minimum hydro, solar, RE and wind capacities (Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Singapore, Viet Nam) and coal caps (Myanmar, Viet Nam) are imposed, several binding exactly in 2035. With no grid expansion, every country must meet these constraints from domestic resources, so they shape each national mix directly.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: Absolute emissions caps are imposed as model constraints: Indonesia's power emissions peak at 290 MtCO2eq by 2030 and Singapore's at 60 MtCO2eq in 2030. In BAU's 2035 results Indonesia emits 236.9 Mt and Singapore 24.0 Mt, so neither cap binds at the reported year.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: The model minimises total system cost using DEA technology-catalogue capex and O&M (Viet Nam/Indonesia average applied to all countries), so unit costs decide what is built beyond the policy minimums. Falling costs for solar (0.79 → 0.56 M USD/MW, 2023-2030) and lithium-ion batteries (0.47 → 0.33 M USD/MW) make battery storage the least-cost balancing option when the grid is fixed: BAU builds 68.0 GW of storage, the most of any pathway.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Electricity demand growth is an exogenous driver common to all four TZ-APG pathways and does not differentiate them: country CAGRs for 2023-2035 range from 1.6% (Myanmar) to 8.1% (Cambodia). Sources are national plans (Cambodia PDMP, Indonesia JETP CIPP, Philippines PDP, Singapore Energy 2050 Committee, Thailand PDP, Viet Nam PDP) and, for Brunei, Lao PDR, Malaysia and Myanmar, TransitionZero estimates based on historical trends and World Bank, IMF and IIASA population and GDP projections.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Grid topology is the defining assumption: BAU freezes the 31 existing domestic and cross-border routes at current capacity. This blocks resource sharing, so balancing falls on local storage (68.0 GW) and gas (138.7 GW), and fixed Lao exports flow mainly to Thailand (Lao→Thailand North 47.5 TWh). This is an infrastructure-design assumption that fits no other named driver.

dependencies.dependency_description: BAU's renewable build-out is driven by national targets, such as RE shares in Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines and capacity minimums in Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Singapore and Viet Nam. With a fixed grid, each country meets its targets domestically. National power plans are the only policy lever for grid decarbonisation; regional instruments play no role. Several constraints bind exactly in 2035, e.g. Lao hydro at 13,000 MW and Viet Nam onshore wind at 21,880 MW.

BAU keeps today's bilateral, largely unidirectional trade from export-dedicated plants under long-term offtake agreements, so it needs no new market rules. The report's calls for market design, grid codes and technical standards (APG phase 3) concern regional integration, not this status-quo grid.

With transmission frozen at today's 31 routes, BAU meets demand and targets through local balancing infrastructure. It needs 68.0 GW of battery storage, the most of any pathway (Viet Nam 36.3 GW, Indonesia 22.9 GW). Storage build-out is the binding infrastructure dependency; dispatch is modelled in 2-hour blocks, which captures intraday storage cycling.

Lithium-ion battery storage is the only new technology in the palette, and BAU relies on it most, building 68.0 GW by 2035. Its capex falls from 0.47 to 0.33 M USD/MW (2023-2030) in the cost inputs. Nuclear, CCUS and hydrogen/ammonia co-firing are excluded from v1.

RE build is capped by node-level technical potentials, and without new links each country relies on domestic resources. Singapore's very limited RE potential leaves it dependent on gas (10.8 GW CCGT) and the existing Malaysian link (5.4 TWh). Fuel is priced as one ASEAN-wide marginal cost, so import dependence (Singapore imports 100% of its fossil fuel) is not reflected in costs.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: Derived: node emissions ÷ node generation, 2035 (ASEAN 0.398 t/MWh). Generation-based, excludes imports. Gas basket and emissions scope not stated (report labels MtCO2eq). Grid-to-grid node model; plant data omits most rooftop/small-scale solar; no captive series.

Total power-system emissions by node, Mt, 2035 (ASEAN 836.8 Mt). GHG basket and emissions scope not stated; report charts label MtCO2eq. Grid-to-grid node model; plant data omits most rooftop/small-scale solar; no captive series.

Installed MW by node and technology, 2035. Storage = lithium-ion battery, separate column, MW only (no MWh). Pumped-storage hydro is included in hydropower, not separated. Coal limited to plants operating or under construction in 2023. Plant data omits most rooftop/small-scale solar; no captive series.

Annual GWh by node and technology, 2035 (ASEAN 2,100.5 TWh). Generation within each node; imports/exports shown separately in transmission trade. Plant data omits most rooftop/small-scale solar; no captive series.
Derived from generation by technology (share of node/country/ASEAN total), 2035. Same on-grid boundary as Generation; excludes imported electricity from the mix of the importing country.

Line-level trade (GWh), capacity (MW) and capex (USD bn) between the 24 nodes. 31 existing routes at fixed capacity; trade only, capex 'NA'. Lines act as combined interfaces between node centre-points; HVAC/HVDC by distance; no distribution grid; no trade with China; no wheeling charges.

Capital (USD/MW), fixed O&M (USD/MW-yr), variable (USD/MWh) and fuel (USD/MWh) costs per country and technology, incl. Li-ion battery and HVAC/HVDC/subsea transmission. DEA Viet Nam/Indonesia average applied to all countries; single ASEAN fuel prices.
Systems cost by node = generator capex 2023-2035 plus 2035 opex (USD bn); blends capex with one year of opex. No transmission investment (no new lines).

Static technical lifetimes (coal 30 yr, gas and oil 40 yr, hydro 50 yr, solar 25 yr, wind 27 yr). No early-retirement constraint; coal capacity identical across all four pathways (101.8 GW in 2035 vs 98.4 GW in 2023 incl. under-construction plants).
